Author: @MegaB1tez
Content:
Chicken ice cream did exist It came from a book we have that I believe is from the 1950’s. The title is "Secrets of Making Frozen Desserts". All the recipes in the cookbook require an "ice cream freezer" (ice cream maker). So when it says "freeze", they mean in an ice cream maker, not just in the freezer.

Chicken mousse
2 cups chicken, chopped fine
1 cup chicken stock
2 cups heavy cream
1 tablespoon powdered gelatine
1 teaspoon salt
1/4 teaspoon black pepper
1/8 teaspoon cayenne pepper
1/8 teaspoon nutmeg
1 tablespoon cold water
Chop chicken to almost a paste and press it through a sieve. Season with salt, peppers, and nutmeg. Heat chicken stock and add gelatine which has been softened in the cold water, mix with chicken. Whip cream and add. Freeze.

I've just read a REALLY good book discussing the development and history of refrigeration - not just the fridge in the kitchen, like the whole cold chain and how we eventually got where we are now. It's incredible how much our food choices are impacted by having cold "on tap." And in those early days ice cream was a huge status symbol, just as much as it was for the Romans to have ice and snow for dinner parties.
Given how awful hot it is this summer in the Deep South, I am SO GRATEFUL that ice cream is cheap nowadays, haha!! And I just might dig out my own ice cream maker and throw together some peach ice cream myself. Or canteloupe since those're available right now too.

Author: @Just1Nora
Content:
Peach is one of my all-time favorite ice cream flavors. I live in peach country, and when I was a kid, we used to occasionally drive about an hour away to a peach stand on a peach orchard and they made the best peach ice cream with their own peaches. We'd bring home peaches, sweet corn, and other produce, and it was always amazing. Peaches on vanilla ice cream is one of my favorite ways to eat them. 
The mold looks to be aluminum, and a few seconds of contact with skin should warm the mold enough to make it release. I have an old paddle style aluminum ice cream scoop that I believed belonged to my grandmother. I used it last night, in fact! 😅 Aluminum conducts heat well and can absorb a lot of it, so it's perfect for ice cream scoops and spoons because the ice cream softens on contact and doesn't stick making it easier to scoop, AND your hands don't get cold like with stainless steel. I have a condition called Reynauds, and when my hands and feet get cold, they become very painful, and they are difficult to warm back up without external heat, and my aluminum scoop keeps my hands from getting cold. I still have an aluminum scoop from my childhood that is smaller to make cone-sized scoops, and it has a trigger to dislodge the scoop, but I prefer the simple, easy to clean, paddle scoop.

FROM WIKIPEDIA: 

Formation
Ambergris is formed from a secretion of the bile duct in the intestines of the sperm whale, and can be found floating on the sea or washed up on coastlines. It is sometimes found in the abdomens of dead sperm whales.[7] Because the beaks of giant squids have been discovered within lumps of ambergris, scientists have hypothesized that the substance is produced by the whale's gastrointestinal tract to ease the passage of hard, sharp objects that it may have eaten.[citation needed]

Ambergris is passed like fecal matter. It is speculated that an ambergris mass too large to be passed through the intestines is expelled via the mouth, but this remains under debate.[10] Another theory states that an ambergris mass is formed when the colon of a whale is enlarged by a blockage from intestinal worms and cephalopod parts resulting in the death of the whale and the mass being excreted into the sea.[11] Ambergris takes years to form. Christopher Kemp, the author of Floating Gold: A Natural (and Unnatural) History of Ambergris, says that it is only produced by sperm whales, and only by an estimated one percent of them. Ambergris is rare; once expelled by a whale, it often floats for years before making landfall.[12] The slim chances of finding ambergris and the legal ambiguity involved led perfume makers away from ambergris, and led chemists on a quest to find viable alternatives.[13]

Ambergris is found primarily in the Atlantic Ocean and on the coasts of South Africa; Brazil; Madagascar; the East Indies; The Maldives; China; Japan; India; Australia; New Zealand; and the Molucca Islands. Most commercially collected ambergris comes from the Bahamas in the Atlantic, particularly New Providence. In 2021, fishermen found a 127 kg (280-pound) piece of ambergris off the coast of Yemen, valued at US$1.5 million.[14] Fossilised ambergris from 1.75 million years ago has also been found.[15]

Actually came across an old recipe that my Granny made at Christmas. As this was strictly an adults only dessert, mum slipped me a small paper cup with a small spoonful. 

I do remember the taste of sweet cherries and real vanilla bean, but the brandy was surprisingly smooth. 

If I remember correctly:
1 quart of sliced and pitted cherries.
2 vanilla bean pods.
1 1/2 cups of good quality Brandy.

If you want to be strictly historic, use an old hand crank ice cream machine .  But the new electric machines work just as well. 

Once it’s done, the special holiday mould was taken out of the freezer. The bottom of the mould was decorated with sliced cherries. The soft serve was gently poured over the cherries. Then it was covered  and frozen on Christmas Eve, so it was ready for Christmas dinner. 

Edited because I made a couple of mistakes in the recipe.

Author: @beesknees947
Content:
To determine if metal contains lead, you can use a lead test kit, which typically involves applying a solution to the metal and observing for a color change. Alternatively, you can assess the metal's properties like density, softness, and reaction to magnets to infer its composition. 
Here's a more detailed breakdown:
1. Lead Test Kits:
How they work:
Lead test kits contain solutions that react with lead, producing a color change on a test strip or swab. 
Where to find them:
You can purchase lead test kits at hardware stores or online. 
Types of tests:
Swab tests: A swab is rubbed on the metal and then tested for a color change, indicating the presence of lead. 
Solution tests: A solution is applied to the metal and observed for a color change. 
Limitations:
Swab tests only detect lead on the surface and may not reveal lead content deeper within the metal. 
Some tests may give false positives. 
Tests don't provide a precise measurement of the amount of lead. 
2. Assessing Metal Properties:
Density: Lead is significantly denser than many other metals, like aluminum or iron. If a metal is noticeably heavier than expected, it may contain lead. 
Softness: Lead is a very soft metal and can be scratched with a fingernail. 
Magnetism: Lead is not magnetic, so if a metal attracts a magnet, it's unlikely to be mostly lead. 
Appearance: Lead can have a dull, grayish appearance. 
Corrosion: Lead doesn't corrode easily, so a metal that corrodes quickly is likely not lead. 
3. Chemical Spot Tests (for advanced users):
HCl and Sodium Rhodizonate: Dilute hydrochloric acid is applied to the metal, followed by sodium rhodizonate. A blue/purple color change indicates lead. 
Safety: These tests require caution due to the use of chemicals. 
Important Considerations:
Always follow the instructions provided with any lead test kit. 
If you suspect lead contamination in a potentially hazardous material (e.g., paint, plumbing), consult with a professional for proper testing and remediation.

Content: Ambergris is super interesting. It's actually the sperm whale's body's protection against the sharp beaks of the squid they eat. Their bodies wrap them in mucus, they crap it out and then it floats and bakes in the sun for a couple of years and then washes up on the beach. Vanilla is a new world crop and they actually used to use Ambergris in many of the recipes that later called for vanilla. It's also a great fixative with an interesting scent and so was massive in perfumery until synthetic alternatives took over due to cost and availability of Ambergris.
